body: In December 1912 Charles Dawson and Arthur Smith Woodward **laid** before the Geological Society a **jaw** and pieces of a **cranium** from a **gravel** **pit** at Piltdown. The **skull** was human, the jaw **ape**-like, the **pairing** **unheard** of. Together they made the missing link, and made it English. Britain had its **forebear**. Doubt came at once. In 1913 David Waterston wrote in *Nature* that this was an ape **jawbone** **paired** with a human skull; Boule **echoed** him in 1915, Miller in Washington. In 1923 the **anatomist** Franz Weidenreich reported a modern skull with an **orangutan** **mandible**, its **teeth** **abraded**. He was right, and **ignored** for a **generation**. **Anatomy** could not settle it: the **hinge** where jaw met skull was broken away, so the two could never be **fitted** and **tested**. Each side read the same plaster **casts** and X-ray **images**, seeing what it expected. **Dissent** and **acclaim** drew on one set of **bones**; the argument had no **arbiter**. In 1949 chemistry supplied one: Kenneth Oakley applied a **fluorine** test. **Buried** bone **absorbs** **fluoride** from **groundwater**, and the longer it **lies** the more it **holds**. Refined by 1953, it read 0.03 to 0.04 per cent in the jaw, the **vault** 0.1. The pieces had not **rested** in one ground for the same **duration**. Oakley, Weiner and Le Gros Clark went further. Under **magnification** the **molars** showed **file** **grooves**: straight **scratches** where chewing leaves **uneven** wear. **Drilling** proved the colour skin-deep: iron and chromic acid matching Piltdown stone. For forty-one years the **inquiry** was what the bones **resembled**; the test asked how long each had **lain**, and only that question had a number.
